Contraception (Debate)
kon-truh-SEP-shun
noun (Christian ethics)
The substantive Christian-ethical debate over the moral permissibility of contraception (the deliberate prevention of conception). Positions range from the Roman Catholic prohibition of all artificial contraception, through the patriarchal-Reformed quiverfull-influenced openness-to-children position, to the broad-Protestant acceptance of contraception within marriage.

📖 Biblical Definition

The substantive Christian-ethical debate over the moral permissibility of contraception (the deliberate prevention of conception within marriage). The principal positions: (1) Roman Catholic prohibition: all artificial contraception is intrinsically immoral (Humanae Vitae, 1968); only natural family planning (periodic abstinence) is permitted; the procreative and unitive purposes of the marital act may not be deliberately separated. (2) The quiverfull / openness-to-children position: influential in patriarchal-Reformed circles; children are an unqualified covenant blessing (Psalm 127:3-5), the creation mandate to be fruitful is unrescinded (Genesis 1:28), and the deliberate prevention of conception substitutes human management for divine providence over the womb. (3) The broad-Protestant acceptance: contraception within marriage is a matter of Christian liberty and prudential stewardship, distinct from abortion (the prevention of conception is morally different from the destruction of an existing person). A substantive sub-question is the distinction between contraceptive methods (which prevent conception) and abortifacient methods (which prevent the implantation of an already-conceived embryo, thereby destroying a human person); the patriarchal-Reformed reader holds firmly that abortifacient methods are gravely wrong on the personhood-from-conception view, regardless of his position on non-abortifacient contraception. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the contraception debate with substantive seriousness: children are a covenant blessing to be received from the LORD; the creation mandate and the multigenerational-faithfulness vision counsel substantive openness to children; the deliberate, comprehensive, lifelong prevention of children within marriage (treating children as a burden to be avoided) contradicts the biblical vision; abortifacient methods are gravely wrong; but the prudential spacing of children and the substantive trust in the LORD's ordering of the womb are matters on which substantive patriarchal-Reformed Christians hold a range of positions.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Christian-ethical debate over the moral permissibility of contraception; positions: Roman Catholic prohibition of all artificial contraception, the quiverfull openness-to-children position, the broad-Protestant acceptance within marriage; substantive distinction between contraceptive and abortifacient methods.

CONTRACEPTION (DEBATE), n. (Christian ethics) The debate over the moral permissibility of contraception within marriage. Positions: (1) Roman Catholic prohibition (Humanae Vitae 1968; all artificial contraception intrinsically immoral; only natural family planning permitted). (2) Quiverfull / openness-to-children position (children an unqualified covenant blessing, Psalm 127:3-5; creation mandate unrescinded, Genesis 1:28; deliberate prevention substitutes human management for divine providence over the womb). (3) Broad-Protestant acceptance (contraception a matter of Christian liberty and prudential stewardship, distinct from abortion). Substantive distinction: contraceptive methods (prevent conception) vs. abortifacient methods (destroy an already-conceived embryo, gravely wrong on the personhood-from-conception view).

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 1:28 — "And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it."

Psalm 127:3-5 — "Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward. As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them."

Genesis 38:9-10 — "And Onan knew that the seed should not be his; and it came to pass, when he went in unto his brother's wife, that he spilled it on the ground, lest that he should give seed to his brother. And the thing which he did displeased the LORD: wherefore he slew him also."

Psalm 139:13 — "For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The contraception debate is substantive within the Christian tradition; the patriarchal-Reformed reader holds firmly that abortifacient methods are gravely wrong and that the comprehensive lifelong avoidance of children contradicts the biblical vision, while substantive positions on non-abortifacient contraception vary.

expand to see more

The contraception debate is a substantive intra-Christian discussion on which substantive positions vary. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds several substantive convictions firmly while recognizing the range of positions on others. Held firmly: (1) children are a covenant blessing to be received from the LORD (Psalm 127:3-5), not a burden to be comprehensively avoided; (2) the creation mandate to be fruitful and multiply (Genesis 1:28) is unrescinded; (3) the multigenerational-faithfulness vision counsels substantive openness to children; (4) abortifacient methods (which destroy an already-conceived embryo) are gravely wrong on the personhood-from-conception view; (5) the contemporary anti-natalist contraceptive mentality (treating children as an obstacle to self-fulfillment, career, and lifestyle) contradicts the biblical vision. Positions vary among substantive patriarchal-Reformed Christians on: the prudential spacing of children; the use of non-abortifacient contraception within an overall posture of openness to children; the precise application of the Onan narrative (Genesis 38:9-10, whose primary sin was the refusal of the levirate duty, though the narrative bears on the broader question). The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the debate with substantive seriousness, holding the biblical openness-to-children vision firmly while recognizing the range of substantive positions on the prudential questions.
